power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .063", Sentence = "No statistically significant group differences were detected for straight-source ISP, F(3, 804) = 2.44, p = .063, η² = .01."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Sexual prejudice, the negative attitudes towards people on the basis of their sexual orientation (Herek, 2000; Herek & McLemore, 2013), can shape both how sexual minority people are treated and how they evaluate their own sexuality.
text.formatted: Sexual prejudice, the negative attitudes towards people on the basis of their sexual orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Herek, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Herek & McLemore, 2013)</ref>, can shape both how sexual minority people are treated and how they evaluate their own sexuality.

text.text: Minority stress theory identifies prejudice, discrimination, and rejection as sources of additional stress associated with a minoritised sexual or gender identity, with consequences for psychological wellbeing (Brooks, 1981; Meyer, 1995; Testa et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Minority stress theory identifies prejudice, discrimination, and rejection as sources of additional stress associated with a minoritised sexual or gender identity, with consequences for psychological wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brooks, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Meyer, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Testa et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: One process through which this social devaluation can become personally consequential is internalised sexual prejudice (ISP): the incorporation of negative attitudes towards minority sexualities into a person's evaluations of their own sexual identity (Herek, 2009).
text.formatted: One process through which this social devaluation can become personally consequential is internalised sexual prejudice (ISP): the incorporation of negative attitudes towards minority sexualities into a person's evaluations of their own sexual identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Herek, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Although ISP is experienced within the individual, its foundations are social.

This distinction is central to minority stress theory, which locates disparities in psychological wellbeing in the stigma and disadvantage associated with a minoritised sexual identity, rather than in that identity itself (Frost & Meyer, 2023; Meyer, 2003; Nguyen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This distinction is central to minority stress theory, which locates disparities in psychological wellbeing in the stigma and disadvantage associated with a minoritised sexual identity, rather than in that identity itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Frost & Meyer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Meyer, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nguyen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The psychological significance of ISP has motivated substantial research into its correlates, development, and potential modification.

In their systematic review of longitudinal and intervention studies, Nguyen et al. (2024) examined ISP as a phenomenon that can develop and change over time within people's social and psychological environments.
text.formatted: In their systematic review of longitudinal and intervention studies, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Nguyen et al. (2024)</ref> examined ISP as a phenomenon that can develop and change over time within people's social and psychological environments.

text.text: This perspective places the social context of internalisation at the centre of efforts to understand it.
Yet a potentially important feature of that context is often absent from its assessment: whose negative evaluation is being internalised?

Sexual minority people may encounter sexuality-based prejudice from straight people or from other LGBTQA+ people, as demonstrated in research on anti-bisexual prejudice (Anderson & Maugeri, 2024; Manalastas et al., 2024) and intraminority stress (Dellers et al., 2026; Pachankis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Sexual minority people may encounter sexuality-based prejudice from straight people or from other LGBTQA+ people, as demonstrated in research on anti-bisexual prejudice <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Maugeri, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Manalastas et al., 2024)</ref> and intraminority stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dellers et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Pachankis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The present research examines whether distinguishing internalising responses associated with prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people provides a useful extension to the conceptualisation and measurement of ISP.

The internalisation of sexual prejudice has been studied under several overlapping terms, including internalised homophobia, internalised homonegativity, internalised heterosexism, and internalised sexual stigma.

Although definitions and measures vary across these traditions (Szymanski et al., 2008a (Szymanski et al., , 2008b)), their common concern is how negative social evaluations of minority sexuality become incorporated into people's evaluations of their own sexuality.
text.formatted: Although definitions and measures vary across these traditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Szymanski et al., 2008a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Szymanski et al., , 2008b))</ref>, their common concern is how negative social evaluations of minority sexuality become incorporated into people's evaluations of their own sexuality.

text.text: Crucially, recognising prejudice is not the same as internalising it. Herek et al. (2009) distinguish internalised stigma from experiences of discriminatory treatment and expectations of such treatment.
text.formatted: Crucially, recognising prejudice is not the same as internalising it. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Herek et al. (2009)</ref> distinguish internalised stigma from experiences of discriminatory treatment and expectations of such treatment.

text.text: Sexual minority people may recognise that others devalue their sexuality while rejecting those attitudes and maintaining a positive sexual identity.
The defining feature of ISP is the adoption of that devaluation in relation to the self, rather than awareness of its existence in the social environment.

Existing measures assess ISP through negative feelings about one's sexuality (Mayfield, 2001), difficulties accepting one's sexual identity and associated social discomfort (Lingiardi et al., 2012), and a wish to be heterosexual (Herek et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Existing measures assess ISP through negative feelings about one's sexuality <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Mayfield, 2001)</ref>, difficulties accepting one's sexual identity and associated social discomfort <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lingiardi et al., 2012)</ref>, and a wish to be heterosexual <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Herek et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For example, the internalised homonegativity subscale of the Lesbian, Gay, and Bisexual Identity Scale (Mohr & Kendra, 2011) includes three items assessing whether respondents would prefer to be straight.
text.formatted: For example, the internalised homonegativity subscale of the Lesbian, Gay, and Bisexual Identity Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mohr & Kendra, 2011)</ref> includes three items assessing whether respondents would prefer to be straight.

text.text: These measures capture negative evaluations of one's own sexuality but do not assess whether respondents associate these feelings with prejudice from straight people, other
LGBTQ+ people, or both.
Consequently, the resulting scores provide information about the extent of ISP while leaving its source unspecified.
This reflects a distinction between how ISP is theorised and the information retained in its measurement.

Minority stress and sexual stigma theories explicitly locate internalisation within a stigmatising social environment (Herek & McLemore, 2013; Meyer, 2003; Meyer, 2010), whereas measures such as the LGBIS assess the resulting self-evaluation without specifying its source (Herek et al., 2009; Mohr & Kendra, 2011).
text.formatted: Minority stress and sexual stigma theories explicitly locate internalisation within a stigmatising social environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Herek & McLemore, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Meyer, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Meyer, 2010)</ref>, whereas measures such as the LGBIS assess the resulting self-evaluation without specifying its source <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Herek et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Mohr & Kendra, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: A source-unspecified assessment is useful when the research question concerns overall ISP, but it is less informative when the question concerns whether people associate their negative sexualidentity evaluations with different interpersonal or social contexts.
For example, two people with similar overall ISP scores might report different internalising responses to rejection from straight and other LGBTQ+ people.
Measuring these responses separately would allow researchers to examine variation that an overall score cannot directly represent.

Research on anti-bisexual prejudice provides a clear precedent for distinguishing the sources of sexual prejudice. Brewster and Moradi (2010) developed the Anti-Bisexual Experiences Scale, to assess perceived prejudicial treatment from heterosexual people separately from treatment by lesbian and gay people.
text.formatted: Research on anti-bisexual prejudice provides a clear precedent for distinguishing the sources of sexual prejudice. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Brewster and Moradi (2010)</ref> developed the Anti-Bisexual Experiences Scale, to assess perceived prejudicial treatment from heterosexual people separately from treatment by lesbian and gay people.

text.text: Respondents evaluate parallel experiences involving assumptions of sexual orientation instability, sexual irresponsibility, and interpersonal hostility under each source frame.
This approach allows researchers to examine whether similar forms of prejudice are experienced differently depending on who expresses them.
Subsequent work has also examined source-specific binegativity in relation to internalised binegativity (Arriaga & Parent, 2019).
text.formatted: Subsequent work has also examined source-specific binegativity in relation to internalised binegativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arriaga & Parent, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In that research, however, the source distinction concerns the prejudice experienced, but not the internalisation of prejudice.
This leaves open whether the negative self-evaluations associated with those experiences can themselves be meaningfully distinguished by source.
There are theoretical reasons to expect the source of prejudice to matter.
LGBTQA+ communities can provide opportunities for belonging, recognition, and affirmation of identities that are devalued elsewhere.

In qualitative research with LGBQ adults, Cavarra et al. (2025) found that participants described support from similar others as facilitating selfacceptance and pride, while judgement and exclusion within these communities could undermine identity affirmation.
text.formatted: In qualitative research with LGBQ adults, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cavarra et al. (2025)</ref> found that participants described support from similar others as facilitating selfacceptance and pride, while judgement and exclusion within these communities could undermine identity affirmation.

text.text: Building on these findings, we propose that rejection from other LGBTQA+ people may challenge expectations of acceptance from those who might otherwise provide support and understanding.
Such rejection may therefore concern both the negative evaluation itself and a threatened source of belonging and affirmation.
This provides a reason to examine whether people associate different internalising responses with prejudice from straight and other LGBTQA+ people.
The present research examines whether distinguishing the social sources associated with internalisation provides a useful extension to the conceptualisation and measurement of ISP.
We define source-specific ISP as negative attitudes and feelings concerning one's sexual identity that individuals associate with sexuality-based prejudice from a specified social source.
This approach extends the source differentiation used in research on experienced prejudice (Brewster & Moradi, 2010) to the assessment of internalisation.
text.formatted: This approach extends the source differentiation used in research on experienced prejudice <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brewster & Moradi, 2010)</ref> to the assessment of internalisation.

text.text: To our knowledge, existing measures have not assessed equivalent internalising responses separately in relation to prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people.
To address this gap, we developed the Source-Specific Internalised Sexual Prejudice Scale (SS-ISP).
Respondents evaluate the same items under two stems describing sexualitybased prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people, respectively.
This parallel format holds the content of the responses constant while varying the specified source, allowing us to examine whether people distinguish their internalising responses by source.
The measure therefore assesses the connections people report between prejudice from particular others and their evaluations of their own sexuality.

The research programme adopts best-practice guidelines for psychometric scale development (Boateng et al., 2018) and comprises four studies examining the content, structure, measurement invariance, initial validity, and temporal stability of the SS-ISP.
text.formatted: The research programme adopts best-practice guidelines for psychometric scale development <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Boateng et al., 2018)</ref> and comprises four studies examining the content, structure, measurement invariance, initial validity, and temporal stability of the SS-ISP.

text.text: Study 1 evaluated the relevance of candidate items through ratings from researchers familiar with discrimination and LGBTQA+ research.
Study 2 explored the factor structure of the retained items in a sample of gay men and examined the internal consistency of the resulting dimensions.
Study 3 evaluated this structure in an independent, broader LGBTQA+ sample.

It also examined measurement invariance across cisgender gay men, cisgender lesbian women, cisgender bisexual men, and cisgender bisexual women, alongside exploratory comparisons of their source-specific scores.
Study 3 further examined associations with an adapted version of the LGBIS internalised homonegativity subscale (Mohr & Kendra, 2011) and concurrent psychological distress.
text.formatted: Study 3 further examined associations with an adapted version of the LGBIS internalised homonegativity subscale <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mohr & Kendra, 2011)</ref> and concurrent psychological distress.

text.text: We expected positive associations with the LGBIS because both measures assess negative evaluations of one's sexuality, and with distress because of the role of ISP within minority stress theory (Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: We expected positive associations with the LGBIS because both measures assess negative evaluations of one's sexuality, and with distress because of the role of ISP within minority stress theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: We also examined whether the two source-specific dimensions jointly accounted for additional variance in distress beyond the LGBIS, providing an initial assessment of incremental criterion-related validity.
Study 4 examined test-retest reliability and temporal stability.
Participants from Study 3 were re-invited to complete the SS-ISP approximately 12 months after their initial assessment.
This follow-up assesses whether individuals' relative standing on each sourcespecific dimension was maintained over time.

Because ISP may change alongside people's experiences and social circumstances, stability over this interval provides evidence about the persistence of the measured responses without implying that individual scores necessarily remain unchanged.
We formed the following predictions:  H1: Content Validity (Study 1).
The candidate items would be rated as relevant to ISP when presented in relation to prejudice from both straight people and other LGBTQA+ people.

Responses to the retained items would show a positively correlated two-factor structure corresponding to straight-source and LGBTQA+-source ISP in Study 2, and this structure would demonstrate acceptable fit in an independent sample in Study 3.
Both source-specific ISP dimensions would be positively associated with scores on the adapted LGBIS internalised homonegativity subscale.
 H4: Concurrent Validity (Study 3).
Both source-specific ISP dimensions would be positively associated with concurrent psychological distress.

The two source-specific ISP dimensions would jointly account for additional variance in concurrent psychological distress beyond that accounted for by the adapted LGBIS internalised homonegativity subscale.
Scores on each source-specific ISP dimension would be positively associated across the 12-month interval.
Measurement invariance and between-group differences were examined as additional research aims, without specifying a directional ordering of group means.
Study 1 developed and evaluated items assessing negative attitudes and feelings about one's sexual identity in response to prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people.
Consistent with H1, we expected the candidate items to be judged relevant to ISP under both source frames.
A central consideration was retaining parallel item content across sources, allowing subsequent studies to examine source differentiation without introducing differences in the items assessed.
Researchers were recruited through an email distributed to the BLINDED FOR REVIEW networking group.
Eligibility required self-reported familiarity with both discrimination and LGBTQA+ research.

Respondents rated their familiarity with research on "discrimination, prejudice, rejection, stigma, and/or harassment experiences" and "LGBTQA+ identity and/or sexuality" on scales ranging from 1 (not at all familiar) to 7 (very familiar).
A rating of at least 5 on both items was required for inclusion.
Fifteen researchers participated, all of whom met these eligibility criteria.
Familiarity was high for both discrimination research (M = 6.27, SD = 0.85) and LGBTQA+ research (M = 6.20, SD = 0.83).
Participants included master's students (6.7%), doctoral candidates (26.7%), early-career academics (26.7%), mid-career academics (26.7%), and late-career academics (13.3%).

The research team developed an initial pool of eight candidate items, each presented under two source frames (16 item presentations), informed by minority stress theory (Brooks, 1981; Meyer, 2003), reviews of internalised stigma and its measurement (Nguyen et al., 2024; Szymanski et al., 2008b), and existing ISP measures (Herek et al., 2009; Mayfield, 2001; Mohr & Kendra, 2011).

text.text: Two items did not meet the criterion consistently.
"I feel negative about myself" fell below the threshold under both the straight and LGBTQA+ stems (both CVRs = .47).
"My identity as a [X] feels less valid" met the criterion under the LGBTQA+ stem (CVR = .73), but not the straight stem (CVR = .33).
Both items were removed from each source frame, preserving parallel content across the two assessments.
This yielded six retained items presented under each stem, producing a 12-item measure for subsequent evaluation.
The findings provided partial support for H1: six of the eight candidate responses met the relevance criterion under both source frames.
Study 2 examined the factor structure and internal consistency of the items retained in Study 1 in a sample of gay men.
Consistent with H2, we expected responses to show two related factors corresponding to straight-source and LGBTQA+-source ISP.

Gay men were recruited through Prolific, with no restrictions on country of birth or residence.

text.text: Of the 347 initial responses, exclusions comprised duplicate responses (n = 5), respondents who did not identify as cisgender or transgender men (n = 4), respondents who did not identify as gay (n = 25), failed attention checks (n = 35), and requests to withdraw responses following survey completion (n = 2).

Although internalised sexual prejudice (ISP) is experienced within the individual, its foundations are social.
The present research examined whether retaining information about the social source associated with internalisation provides a useful extension to its measurement.

Across four studies, the findings provided initial support for the Source-Specific Internalised Sexual Prejudice Scale (SS-ISP), which assesses equivalent internalising responses in relation to prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people.
Six parallel items met the content relevance criterion under both source frames, and exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported two related dimensions organised by source.
Study 3 supported measurement invariance across four sexual-identity and gender groups and provided initial evidence of convergent, concurrent, and incremental validity.
Group differences emerged for LGBTQA+-source ISP, and an exploratory comparison indicated that this dimension had a stronger adjusted association with psychological distress than straight-source ISP.
Study 4 provided evidence of 12-month temporal stability, indicating that individual differences in both source-specific dimensions persisted over time.
Together, these findings suggest that retaining source information captures meaningful variation in how people associate social devaluation with their evaluations of their own sexuality.
Minority stress and sexual stigma theories locate internalisation within a social environment that devalues minority sexualities (Brooks, 1981; Herek et al., 2009; Meyer, 2003).

text.text: Established measures assess aspects of this process through negative feelings about sexuality, difficulties accepting a sexual-minority identity, and preferences for heterosexuality (Lingiardi et al., 2012; Mohr & Kendra, 2011; Padilla et al., 2025; Szymanski et al., 2008b).

text.text: These assessments provide information about the evaluations people hold, but generally leave unspecified whose prejudice respondents associate with them.
The SS-ISP addresses this omission by assessing equivalent internalising responses separately in relation to prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people.
The parallel item format is central to this contribution.
Each source frame presented the same six responses, allowing source differentiation to be examined without introducing different item content across the two dimensions.
In Study 2, responses were organised into factors corresponding to prejudice from straight people and other LGBTQA+ people.
This structure replicated in Study 3, among a sample that included a broader range of sexual and gender identities.

Although the dimensions were strongly associated, indicating considerable overlap in participants' internalising responses, their separation supports distinguishing the social contexts that respondents associate with negative evaluations of their sexuality.
The findings do not establish that the sources generate independent psychological processes or exhaust the contexts in which internalisation occurs.
Rather, the SS-ISP complements sourceunspecified measures when researchers seek to retain information about these contexts.

Research on anti-bisexual prejudice distinguishes negative treatment from heterosexual and lesbian/gay people (Brewster & Moradi, 2010), while intraminority stress research demonstrates the psychological relevance of pressures within LGBTQA+ communities (Pachankis et al., 2020).

text.text: Together, this research highlights the relevance of prejudice both within and beyond LGBTQA+ communities.
The SS-ISP extends this attention to social source into the assessment of internalising responses, rather than experiences of rejection alone.
The group comparisons further illustrated differences in source-specific ISP.
Across the four cisgender groups examined, no statistically significant differences were detected in straight-source ISP, whereas differences emerged for LGBTQA+-source ISP.
Bisexual women reported higher LGBTQA+-source ISP than lesbian women and gay men, while bisexual men reported higher scores than lesbian women.
However, bisexual men did not differ significantly from gay men, who also reported higher scores than lesbian women.
The pattern therefore does not indicate a uniform difference between bisexual and monosexual participants.

Nevertheless, the findings concerning bisexual participants can be considered alongside evidence of prejudice and bi-erasure within broader sexual-minority communities, including challenges to the legitimacy of bisexuality and bisexual people's belonging (Anderson & Maugeri, 2024; McCole et al., 2025).

text.text: The present findings extend this literature by identifying group differences in the negative feelings about sexuality that respondents associate with within-community rejection.
Support for scalar invariance strengthens the interpretation of these comparisons by supporting comparable measurement across the four groups.
This evidence was limited to cisgender gay men, lesbian women, bisexual men, and bisexual women.
It does not establish equivalent measurement across all populations included within the LGBTQA+ umbrella, nor does it imply that prejudice from other LGBTQA+ people has the same meaning for everyone.
Shared membership of a broad identity category can coexist with differences in recognition, belonging, and acceptance.

Both SS-ISP dimensions were positively associated with LGBIS internalised homonegativity, providing evidence of convergence with an established measure of negative evaluations of one's sexuality (Mohr & Kendra, 2011).

text.text: These correlations were moderate, suggesting that the measures capture overlapping but nonidentical aspects of ISP.

This pattern may reflect differences in both content and framing: the LGBIS subscale emphasises a preference for heterosexuality, whereas the SS-ISP assesses a broader range of negative feelings and self-evaluations that respondents associate with rejection from specified sources.
Both source-specific dimensions were also associated with concurrent psychological distress.

These findings are consistent with the position of ISP within minority stress theory (Brooks, 1981; Meyer, 2003), although the cross-sectional design does not establish the direction of these associations.

text.text: Internalising responses may contribute to distress, distress may influence how people experience and report these responses, or both may be associated with other experiences and circumstances.
The incremental validity findings further indicated that the SS-ISP captured information relevant to distress beyond that provided by the conventional measure.
Adding the SS-ISP dimensions increased the variance explained in concurrent distress from approximately 3% to 13%.
Both SS-ISP dimensions retained positive associations with distress in the final model, whereas the association with LGBIS internalised homonegativity was no longer statistically significant.
The exploratory comparison provided further, albeit preliminary, evidence of the potential significance of distinguishing sources.
LGBTQA+-source ISP showed a stronger association with concurrent distress than straight-source ISP after accounting for their overlap and conventional ISP.

Because the two dimensions assess the same responses on the same scale, this finding suggests that their reported social context may be relevant to understanding differences in their associations with wellbeing.
In particular, it draws attention to negative evaluations of one's sexuality linked to rejection from people within a potential identity community.
Although exploratory and requiring replication, the finding highlights a distinction that source-unspecified measures cannot directly assess.
One possible explanation concerns the relational significance of rejection within a potential identity community.
Other LGBTQA+ people may provide recognition and affirmation of identities that are devalued elsewhere, making their rejection consequential for both self-evaluation and expectations of belonging.
This interpretation is consistent with accounts of community support and exclusion described by Cavarra et al. (2025).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with accounts of community support and exclusion described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cavarra et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, neither expectations of acceptance nor threatened belonging were directly assessed in the present studies.
The exploratory finding provides an initial basis for investigating these possibilities, with replication needed before drawing broader conclusions about differences between sources.

Study 4 provided evidence of moderate test-retest reliability for both source-specific dimensions over 12 months, with positive correlations across assessments and no statistically significant mean-level differences.
The 12-month interval provides a context for interpreting temporal stability.
ISP can develop and change alongside social and psychological experiences, as reflected in longitudinal and intervention research (Nguyen et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: ISP can develop and change alongside social and psychological experiences, as reflected in longitudinal and intervention research <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Nguyen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nguyen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, correspondence between assessments reflects the persistence of individual differences across a period in which genuine change is also possible.
Several limitations qualify the conclusions.
First, the SS-ISP assesses respondents' reported connections between rejection and their evaluations of their own sexuality.
It does not independently establish the historical origin of those evaluations or demonstrate that a particular source caused their internalisation.
The conditional wording may capture relatively immediate or context-dependent responses to rejection alongside more enduring negative self-attitudes.
Further research could examine how these source-linked responses relate to persistent ISP and how they vary across everyday encounters.
Second, the source categories are broad.
Straight people and other LGBTQA+ people encompass different relationships, identities, and social positions.
Rejection from a close friend, partner, family member, or unfamiliar person may carry different meanings even within the same source category.
Future research could adapt the parallel format to distinguish more specific sources, such as straight men and women, or cisgender and transgender lesbian, gay, and bisexual people.

Examining these distinctions would respond to calls for research that attends to differences within broad LGBTQA+ categories rather than assuming shared experiences across subpopulations (Hässler et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Examining these distinctions would respond to calls for research that attends to differences within broad LGBTQA+ categories rather than assuming shared experiences across subpopulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hässler et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such adaptations could clarify which interpersonal contexts are associated with internalising responses, although their interpretation and measurement properties would require evaluation.
The current categories may also overlap, because heterosexuality and membership of the LGBTQA+ umbrella are not mutually exclusive.
They should therefore be understood as the source frames presented to respondents, rather than exhaustive or mutually exclusive classifications.
The measure also does not separately assess how often respondents encounter rejection from each source.
A higher score may reflect differences in exposure, the perceived significance of particular experiences, or the strength of the internalising response.
Future research that assesses both source-specific rejection and internalisation could help distinguish these possibilities.
This would be particularly useful for understanding group differences and identifying whether changes in social experiences precede changes in source-specific ISP.
The samples also impose limitations on generalisability.
Studies 2 and 3 recruited participants through Prolific, with Study 2 restricted to gay men and Study 3 predominantly comprising White participants residing in the United States.
Study 4 involved a subset of Study 3 participants who completed the follow-up assessment, raising the possibility of selective attrition.
Further validation in more diverse samples is therefore warranted.
Finally, the present studies provide initial rather than exhaustive validity evidence.
Content evaluation relied on researcher ratings, and cognitive interviews and broader community input could clarify how respondents understand the stems and items.

Validation against additional outcomes and related constructs could further establish the boundaries between source-specific ISP, rejection sensitivity, identity-related distress, and other responses to prejudice.
Such work would help identify when retaining source information provides the greatest benefit for understanding sexual minority people's experiences.
The present research introduces an approach to ISP measurement that retains information about whose prejudice respondents associate with negative evaluations of their own sexuality.

The findings support two related source-specific dimensions, identify variation across sexual identity groups, and provide initial evidence of their relevance to psychological distress beyond a conventional ISP measure.

Assessing these responses separately offers a means of examining internalisation with greater attention to its reported social context, while recognising that experiencing prejudice and incorporating its devaluation into the self remain distinct processes.
